cards.front: Recall a key point about Composition and Framing
cards.back: Composition in photography is about what you INCLUDE and EXCLUDE from the frame — every element should have a purpose.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composition and Framing
cards.back: The rule of thirds places subjects at intersection points for dynamic balance; centre placement creates formality or stillness.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composition and Framing
cards.back: Leading lines guide the viewer's eye through the image — roads, fences, rivers, shadows all work as leading lines.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composition and Framing
cards.back: Viewpoint changes meaning: low angle = power; high angle = vulnerability; eye level = neutrality; dutch angle = tension.

cards.front: What should you know about photography exam tips?
cards.back: Show MULTIPLE compositions of the same subject — prove you considered alternatives. Annotate with COMPOSITIONAL vocabulary. Explain the MEANING behind your framing choices. Consider what you EXCLUDED as well as what you included.

Students often make mistakes with this topic. Wrong: Good photography is about having an expensive camera, not about composition. Correct: Composition is MORE important than equipment. A well-composed photo on a phone will always be stronger than a poorly composed photo on an expensive camera. The decisions about what to include, how to frame and where to place elements are what make a photograph
Photograph the same subject from five different viewpoints and using at least three compositional techniques. Create a contact sheet and annotate which composition is most effective and why.

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Composition and Framing
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Composition and Framing using appropriate art vocabulary. Identify techniques, materials and processes accurately.

cards.front: Understanding Composition and Framing in Context
cards.back: Composition and Framing is a fundamental aspect of GCSE Art and Design that connects to all four AQA assessment objectives. Understanding this topic requires both practical skill and contextual knowledge — you must apply techniques effectively AND explain how your work relates to other artists and designers. The AQA specification requires you to develop ideas (AO1), refine work through experimenta

For composition and framing, effective experimentation means testing multiple approaches systematically. Start by researching how professional artists approach composition and framing, replicate their techniques as studies, then adapt and combine approaches to develop your own method. The AQA mark scheme rewards purposeful experimentation — random undocumented attempts score lower than systematic

The AQA assessment objective AO4 requires a ‘personal, meaningful response’ — your work should express your own ideas and viewpoints, not simply replicate what you have seen.
